doc.title: Tom Malone interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2023

title: SNL arranger and music director, and notation software
summary: Malone was SNL arranger for ten years and music director 1981-85; he moved from score paper and copyists to Overture software.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Exactly. They — yeah. We just backed up these guys, and that was — my whole career at Saturday Night Live for ten years I was arranger for ten — I was also the music director from ’81 to ’85. You know Eddie Murphy, Joe Piscopo, Martin Short, Billy Crystal era. I wrote the music to “Hot Tub.” I didn’t write the lyrics but I wrote “Hot Tub” and I produced the pre-record for that scene.
Were you writing with score paper and pencil during this time?

I did. I started out with score paper and I had a copyist. I’d take the stuff at like eleven or twelve at night, take it to the copyist up on the Upper West Side and he would show up in the morning at the show with the parts copies out professionally. Now, ever since computer notation software has come out I do it all in there and it speeds up the process. You know cutting and pasting, it just is so much faster. And I don’t use the copyist anymore, I can lay out the parts quite rapidly and print them out, or email them out, and that’s the way I do it. I use a software called Overture. Most people use Sibelius or Finale. But I helped Overture, I was a beta tester for Overture when they were developing the software and I was using it on the TV shows, so I would find mistakes in the software, send it to the company, they would send me a beta version, and ten or twelve beta versions later they would release a new version to the general public for sale. So I got a very inside view on how this stuff works.
That’s cool because I know Finale has some things that are quite annoying but to be in on the development of it you’re not going to get annoyances when you get the final product.
